explanations.explanation: Christ is the word they use. They say, “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.” They want it said out loud, with no hints and no riddles. Straight answer, no sprinkles on top, friend.
Prophet is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word they use. They say, “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.” They want Jesus to say it straight. Not a hint, not a riddle.

Baptist doesn't show up in their question. They say, “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.” John, who had been baptizing, comes up near the end of this passage, but not here. Hold that thought, friend.

explanations.answer: The works He does in His Father’s name
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.” His works speak up for Him. I think that's a lot like a batch of cookies: you can talk about them all day, but the batch tells the story.

explanations.answer: The crowds who follow Him everywhere
explanations.explanation: Crowds are all over the Gospels, but Jesus doesn't point to them here. He says, “The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.” The witness is what He does, not who is standing around. A big crowd is nice, but it isn't the answer.

explanations.answer: The priests who serve in the temple
explanations.explanation: Jesus is walking in the temple courts, so I see why the priests came to mind. But He never mentions them here. He says, “The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.” The works are the witness.
True, friend. Jesus says, “But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe.” They asked Him to speak plainly, and I think that was plain. Nothing hidden in the dough there.

Jesus actually does say it. His words are, “But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe.” So the statement is true. I think that one was sneaky, friend, like a cookie that looks done but isn't.
Follow is the word. Jesus says, “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.” Listen, known, follow. That's the order, friend.
Praise sounds lovely, but it isn't the word here. Jesus says, “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.” They follow Him. Walking with Him comes first.
Fear isn't in this verse, friend. Jesus says, “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.” He knows them, and they follow. That's the whole picture.

explanations.answer: Snatch them out of His hand
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus says, “No one can snatch them out of My hand.” Then He says it again about the Father's hand. Two hands, friend, and nobody is grabbing anything out of either one.

explanations.answer: Make them grow tired or weak
explanations.explanation: Tired and weak aren't in this passage. Jesus says, “No one can snatch them out of My hand.” The promise is about who holds them. No one pulls them out.

explanations.answer: Keep them from hearing His voice
explanations.explanation: Close, because His voice does come up. Jesus says His sheep listen to His voice (John 10:27). But the thing no one can do is in the next verse: “No one can snatch them out of My hand.” Voice in one verse, hand in the next.

explanations.answer: They pick up stones to stone Him
explanations.explanation: They pick up stones. The text says “again,” so this isn't the first time. Jesus had just said, “I and the Father are one,” and that's when the stones come out. Heavy moment, friend, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: They bow down and worship Him
explanations.explanation: Nobody bows in this scene, friend. The text says, “At this, the Jews again picked up stones to stone Him.” Stones, not knees. It's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: They turn and walk away from Him
explanations.explanation: They don't walk away. The text says they picked up stones to stone Him. A little later they try to seize Him too (John 10:39). It's a tense moment, friend.

explanations.answer: Which of these they are stoning Him for
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus asks, “For which of these do you stone Me?” He lays His good works out and asks about them. I think that's a quiet question, and a hard one to answer with stones in your hands.

explanations.answer: Why they came to the feast this year
explanations.explanation: The feast is happening, but Jesus doesn't ask about it. He says, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?” His question is about the works. Nothing about travel plans, friend.

explanations.answer: Who sent them to the temple courts
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask who sent them. He says, “For which of these do you stone Me?” He's talking about His good works from the Father. The question goes straight to the stones.

Blasphemy is their word. They say, “We are not stoning You for any good work, but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.” That's their reason, in their own words. They don't point to a single good work.

Sorcery isn't what they say. Their words are, “We are not stoning You for any good work, but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.” The word they use is blasphemy. Sorcery never comes up.

Idolatry isn't in their answer, friend. They say, “We are not stoning You for any good work, but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.” Blasphemy is the word they use.

True. Right while Jesus talks about those to whom the word of God came, He says the Scripture cannot be broken. He's pointing them back to their own Law. Friend, I'd keep that line close, because it's a sturdy one.

Jesus does say it. While talking about those to whom the word of God came, He says the Scripture cannot be broken. So the statement is true. I think the card made it sound too good to be true, friend.

Son of God is the answer. Jesus says, “How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God?” He says it plainly, right to their faces. He also calls Himself the One the Father sanctified and sent into the world.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, but Jesus doesn't compare Himself to him here. He says, “How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God?” He calls Himself the Son of God. That's the claim they were upset about.

David, Israel's king, is a great name, but Jesus doesn't use it here. He says, “How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God?” The title He names is Son of God, friend.

explanations.answer: The Father is in Him and He is in the Father
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says the works are so that they may know and understand “…that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.” Even if they don't believe His words, He points them to what He has done. Believe the works, friend.

explanations.answer: The feast was set apart in His honor
explanations.explanation: The Feast of Dedication is where this happens, but Jesus doesn't say the works are about the feast. He says they help people know and understand “…that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.” That's the point of the works.

explanations.answer: The temple courts were built for His coming
explanations.explanation: The temple courts are the setting, but Jesus doesn't say a word about their purpose. He says the works are so they may know and understand “…that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.” That's what the works are for.
They don't hold on to Him. The text says, “At this, they tried again to seize Him, but He escaped their grasp.” They try, and He gets away. So the statement is false, friend.
False is right. The text says, “At this, they tried again to seize Him, but He escaped their grasp.” They reach, but they never keep hold. Not one of them.
John it is. Jesus goes back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and He stays there. John is the one who had been baptizing there. Names matter, friend.

Peter, one of Jesus' disciples (John 1:40-42), is a good name to know, but the text doesn't connect him to this place. It says Jesus went to the place where John had first been baptizing. So the name we want is John.
Philip, someone Jesus called to follow Him (John 1:43), isn't named in this verse. The text says Jesus went back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing. John is the one.
It's the other way around. The people say, “Although John never performed a sign…” So John performed no sign at all. The statement is false, friend.
False is right. The people say, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” Never a single sign. And they still trusted his words.

All true. The people say, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” No signs, but his words held up. Friend, I'd love to have a batch of cookies that reliable.
That isn't what they say. Their words are, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” They say it was true. Nothing about it being hard.
Forgotten isn't in their words. They say, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” They remember it, and they call it true. Not forgotten, friend.
That's the ending. The text says, “And many in that place believed in Jesus.” After all those stones and grabbing hands, here are people who believe. I think that's a good place to land, friend.

explanations.answer: Many there try to seize Him
explanations.explanation: That's what happened back in Jerusalem, where they tried to seize Him and He escaped their grasp. Across the Jordan it's different. The text says, “And many in that place believed in Jesus.” Different place, different ending.

explanations.answer: Many there tell Him to leave
explanations.explanation: Nobody tells Him to leave across the Jordan. The text says, “Many came to Him,” and then, “And many in that place believed in Jesus.” They come to Him, and they believe. That's the ending, friend.
